# Block 7: Data cleaning and validation with AI {.unnumbered} :::{.callout-note} **Last verified:** 9 October 2026, against the Claude Code documentation (code.claude.com) and the Posit Assistant documentation (assistant.posit.co, docs version 1.7). Tool behaviour changes quickly; check the linked pages before teaching. ::: Cleaning is where an AI assistant looks most useful and where its mistakes are hardest to see. A cleaning script can run without error, return the right columns and produce plausible values while having treated a missing-value code as a measurement, kept the same animal twice, or dropped a row nobody noticed. None of these raises an error. This block treats cleaning as four artefacts, each with a different owner: | Artefact | Owner | Why | |---|---|---| | Codebook (`docs/codebook.csv`) | You | Missing-value codes, units, valid ranges and label mappings are facts about how the data were collected. They cannot be inferred reliably from the values. | | Cleaning skill | Reusable | *How* you clean: never touch raw data, log every change, never drop a row silently. The same for every dataset. | | Validation and audit scripts | You, or a separate session | Written from the codebook, independently of the cleaning code, so one misunderstanding cannot pass both. | | Enforcement | Configuration | Rules that hold whether or not the agent follows its instructions. | You will work on a version of the voles data with errors planted in it. Your instructor holds the answer key, so at the end you can measure what your pipeline caught and what it missed. *⏱ ~75 minutes* :::{.callout-important} **Why not simply ask the AI to clean the data?** In a 2025 study that gave several language models deliberately polluted tables, the models generally found missing values in standard formats but struggled with codes such as `-1`, rarely detected non-exact duplicates, and performed worse as the proportion of errors rose (Spreafico et al., 2025). The study gave the models a 100-row sample as text in the prompt rather than asking an agent to write and run code, and the models are older than those you will use, so treat it as a map of where to look, not a measure of current tools. The error classes it identifies are the ones planted in this block's data. ::: ## The repository layout ``` repo/ ├── .agents/skills/clean-with-codebook/SKILL.md the skill (single copy) ├── .claude/ │ ├── settings.json permission rules for Claude Code │ └── skills/clean-with-codebook symbolic link to the folder above ├── .gitattributes stops line-ending changes to raw data ├── data/ │ ├── raw/voles_raw.csv never edited by anyone │ └── derived/ cleaning outputs and logs ├── docs/ │ ├── data_note.md the data provider's note │ └── codebook.csv you write this in Step 2 ├── scripts/ │ ├── 00_profile.R provided │ ├── 01_clean.R written by the agent in Step 4 │ ├── 02_validate.R provided │ ├── 03_audit_cleaning.R provided │ └── functions/validate_voles.R provided, or written in Step 3 └── tests/ ├── fixtures/raw_checksum.txt you create this in Step 0 └── test_cleaning.R provided ``` The skill folder is stored once, in `.agents/skills/`, which Posit Assistant and GitHub Copilot both read. Claude Code reads `.claude/skills/` and follows symbolic links, so a link avoids keeping two copies. On macOS or Linux, from the repository root: ```bash mkdir -p .claude/skills ln -s ../../.agents/skills/clean-with-codebook .claude/skills/clean-with-codebook ``` On Windows, symbolic links in git need extra configuration. Copying the folder is acceptable, but you then have two copies to keep in step. ## Step 0: Lock the raw data Everything later depends on the raw file being exactly what the data provider sent. Three controls protect it, and each covers a different route. The [enforced-controls block](11f-enforced-controls.qmd) explains each in more depth. **1. Record a checksum and commit it.** Run this once, yourself: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} raw_path <- here::here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv") writeLines( unname(tools::md5sum(raw_path)), here::here("tests", "fixtures", "raw_checksum.txt") ) ``` ::: Add this line to `.gitattributes` so git does not convert line endings, which would change the checksum on Windows: ``` data/raw/** -text ``` **2. Deny edits in the agent's configuration.** For Claude Code, the project file `.claude/settings.json` contains: ```json { "permissions": { "deny": [ "Edit(/data/raw/**)", "Edit(/docs/codebook.csv)", "Edit(/docs/data_note.md)", "Edit(/scripts/02_validate.R)", "Edit(/scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R)", "Edit(/scripts/functions/**)", "Edit(/tests/**)" ] } } ``` A leading `/` anchors each pattern to the project root. Run `/permissions` to confirm the rules are active. Posit Assistant has no documented path rules for file edits; use the guard hook from the [enforced-controls block](11f-enforced-controls.qmd) instead. **3. Test the control, do not assume it.** Ask the agent to add a comment line to the top of `data/raw/voles_raw.csv`. It should be refused. Then run the tests (Step 5) and confirm the checksum test still passes. :::{.callout-warning} **What each control covers.** The permission rule blocks the agent's file-editing tools. It does not cover commands the agent runs through the shell or R: an R script that the agent runs is a different route. The checksum test catches a change made by *any* route, but only after the fact. On the Copilot cloud agent, where you have no local permission file, the checksum test running in CI plus branch protection is your control. Use both where you can: one prevents, the other detects. ::: :::{.callout-note} **Data governance.** A deny rule on *editing* does not stop data reaching the model provider. If the agent runs a script that prints data, those values enter its context. For personal or confidential data, let the agent work on a synthetic copy and run the final script on the real data yourself, outside the agent's workspace. ::: ## Step 1: Profile the raw data (R, not AI) Profiling is counting, and counting is something you should compute rather than ask a model to estimate. Run the provided script yourself: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/00_profile.R ---- # Purpose: describe the raw file as entered, before any decision is made. # Every column is read as character so codes such as 9999 or -1 appear # exactly as entered. library(tidyverse) library(here) raw_df <- read_csv( here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"), col_types = cols(.default = col_character()) ) # one row per column: missingness, distinct values, numeric range ---- profile_df <- raw_df |> pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "value") |> # suppressWarnings: text values become NA here by design mutate(value_num = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(value))) |> summarise( n_rows = n(), n_missing = sum(is.na(value)), n_distinct = n_distinct(value, na.rm = TRUE), n_numeric = sum(!is.na(value_num)), min_numeric = if (all(is.na(value_num))) NA_real_ else min(value_num, na.rm = TRUE), max_numeric = if (all(is.na(value_num))) NA_real_ else max(value_num, na.rm = TRUE), .by = column ) # every distinct label in the categorical columns ---- labels_df <- raw_df |> select(sex, treatment_arm) |> pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "value") |> count(column, value, sort = TRUE) # identifiers that appear more than once ---- repeated_ids_df <- raw_df |> count(subject_id) |> filter(n > 1) print(profile_df, n = Inf) print(labels_df, n = Inf) print(repeated_ids_df) ``` ::: Keep the output. It is the factual input to Step 2. ## Step 2: Draft the codebook, then audit it :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Draft and audit the codebook :::: ::::{.task-container} **1. Let the AI draft it from the profile alone.** Do not give it the data provider's note yet. ``` Here is a profile of a raw data file. Draft docs/codebook.csv with the columns: column, type, rule, min, max, missing_codes, unit, source. In the source column, state for every entry whether it comes from the profile or is your assumption. Do not write any other file. [paste the output of scripts/00_profile.R] ``` **2. Audit the draft.** Before you open `docs/data_note.md`, answer: - Did the draft list `9999` as a missing-value code, or treat it as a large measurement? - Did it notice that `-1` is a code? - Where did its `min` and `max` come from? A range read off the data includes the errors in the data, so it cannot be used to detect them. Valid ranges must come from the biology or the protocol. **3. Correct it against the data provider's note.** Open `docs/data_note.md` and edit the codebook yourself. Every line should be traceable to the note or to a decision you can defend. :::: :::
``` column,type,rule,min,max,missing_codes,unit,source subject_id,character,"pattern ^V[0-9]{3}$; unique; pad digits to three",,,,,data note sex,character,"allowed M, F; recode male to M, female to F",,,,,data note treatment_arm,character,"allowed Control, Low_dose, High_dose; match case-insensitively",,,,,data note mass_pre_g,double,,15,60,9999,g,data note (range from colony records) mass_post_g,double,,15,60,9999,g,data note (range from colony records) metabolic_rate_post,double,,5,30,-1,,data note (range from equipment) ```
## Step 3: Write the validation rules (independently) Validation rules are transcribed from the codebook, not from the cleaning script. If the same session writes both, a single misunderstanding (for example, that `-1` is a valid reading) passes both. Either use the provided `scripts/functions/validate_voles.R`, or open a **new** session with no access to any cleaning code and prompt: ``` Using only docs/codebook.csv, write scripts/functions/validate_voles.R containing a function validate_voles(data, label) that builds a pointblank agent with one validation step per codebook rule, and interrogates it. Also write voles_col_types(), returning readr column types for the codebook columns, with character as the default for anything else. Do not read or write any other file. ``` Compare what it writes with the reference:
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/functions/validate_voles.R ---- # Rules transcribed from docs/codebook.csv by a human, not by the agent # that writes the cleaning script. voles_col_types <- function() { readr::cols( subject_id = readr::col_character(), sex = readr::col_character(), treatment_arm = readr::col_character(), mass_pre_g = readr::col_double(), mass_post_g = readr::col_double(), metabolic_rate_post = readr::col_double(), .default = readr::col_character() ) } validate_voles <- function(data, label) { data |> pointblank::create_agent(label = label) |> pointblank::col_vals_not_null(columns = c(subject_id, sex, treatment_arm)) |> pointblank::col_vals_regex(columns = subject_id, regex = "^V[0-9]{3}$") |> pointblank::rows_distinct(columns = subject_id) |> pointblank::col_vals_in_set(columns = sex, set = c("M", "F")) |> pointblank::col_vals_in_set( columns = treatment_arm, set = c("Control", "Low_dose", "High_dose") ) |> pointblank::col_vals_between( columns = c(mass_pre_g, mass_post_g), left = 15, right = 60, na_pass = TRUE ) |> pointblank::col_vals_between( columns = metabolic_rate_post, left = 5, right = 30, na_pass = TRUE ) |> pointblank::interrogate() } ``` :::
**Run the rules on the raw data. They should fail.** If raw data pass every rule, either the data are already clean or the rules are too weak, and you should suspect the second. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/02_validate.R ---- library(tidyverse) library(here) source(here("scripts", "functions", "validate_voles.R")) raw_df <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"), col_types = voles_col_types()) validate_voles(raw_df, "Raw data: expected to FAIL") ``` ::: Note which rules fail and how many rows each flags. Every failure is a problem that the cleaning must resolve or log. :::{.callout-warning} `na_pass = TRUE` lets genuine missing values through. It would also let through a cleaning script that replaced *every* mass with `NA`. Validation alone cannot catch over-cleaning; the audit in Step 5 can. ::: ## Step 4: Clean with the skill, plan first The skill holds the procedure; the codebook holds the facts. It sets `disable-model-invocation: true`, so it runs only when you invoke it by name. That is appropriate for a workflow that writes files. :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## `.agents/skills/clean-with-codebook/SKILL.md` ```markdown --- name: clean-with-codebook description: >- Writes or revises a reproducible R cleaning script that applies a human-authored codebook (docs/codebook.csv) to raw tabular data. Use when asked to clean, recode or prepare raw data in a project that has a codebook. Not for exploratory analysis or modelling. disable-model-invocation: true --- # Clean data against a codebook ## Hard constraints 1. Never modify anything under data/raw/. Read raw files with explicit column types. 2. The codebook is the only source of rules. Do not infer units, ranges, missing-value codes or label mappings that the codebook does not state. 3. Do not edit docs/, scripts/functions/, scripts/02_validate.R, scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R or anything under tests/. If a check fails, report it; never change a check to make it pass. 4. Never drop a row silently. Every excluded row goes in the exclusion log with a reason. 5. Every changed cell goes in the cleaning log. 6. A value outside a codebook range that no codebook rule explains is set to NA, logged with rule "out_of_range_query", and listed in the final report. Never correct it by guessing a unit or decimal error. 7. No imputation. 8. Tidyverse style, native pipe, here::here() for all paths. ## Procedure 1. Present a plan before writing anything: every rule you will apply, the codebook row it comes from, and the order. Wait for the user to confirm. 2. If the data contain a value the codebook does not cover, stop and ask. 3. Write scripts/01_clean.R and run it in a fresh R session. 4. Run scripts/02_validate.R on the clean data and run the tests in tests/. Report the results verbatim. ## Outputs (exact columns) - data/derived/voles_clean.csv: the codebook columns plus raw_row, the row number in the raw file. - data/derived/exclusion_log.csv: raw_row, subject_id, reason. - data/derived/cleaning_log.csv: raw_row, subject_id, column, old_value, new_value, rule. ## Final report Row counts in, out and excluded; every value set to NA for query; any gaps in the codebook you found. ``` ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Plan, review, then execute :::: ::::{.task-container} **1.** With your repository committed and clean, switch your assistant to plan mode (in Posit Assistant, `/plan`; in Claude Code, plan mode) and invoke the skill: ``` /clean-with-codebook Clean data/raw/voles_raw.csv using docs/codebook.csv. Start with the plan. ``` **2. Review the plan before approving it.** Check that: - every rule cites a codebook row; - out-of-range values are set to `NA` and queried, not "corrected"; - no file outside `scripts/01_clean.R` and `data/derived/` will be written; - duplicates are handled by a stated rule, with each exclusion logged. **3.** Approve, let it execute, and note every time it stopped to ask you something. A well-behaved agent should stop at least once. :::: ::: ## Step 5: Check the result Four checks, each catching something the others cannot. **1. Validation on clean data should pass.** Run `validate_voles()` on `data/derived/voles_clean.csv`. **2. The tests: raw data unchanged and every row accounted for.** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # tests/test_cleaning.R ---- library(testthat) source(here::here("scripts", "functions", "validate_voles.R")) read_chr <- function(...) { readr::read_csv( here::here(...), col_types = readr::cols(.default = readr::col_character()) ) } test_that("raw data are unchanged", { recorded <- readLines(here::here("tests", "fixtures", "raw_checksum.txt")) current <- unname(tools::md5sum(here::here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"))) expect_identical(current, recorded) }) test_that("every raw row is either in the clean data or in the exclusion log", { raw_df <- read_chr("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv") clean_df <- read_chr("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv") excluded_df <- read_chr("data", "derived", "exclusion_log.csv") expect_equal(nrow(raw_df), nrow(clean_df) + nrow(excluded_df)) expect_setequal( c(clean_df$raw_row, excluded_df$raw_row), as.character(seq_len(nrow(raw_df))) ) expect_false(any(is.na(excluded_df$reason) | excluded_df$reason == "")) }) test_that("clean data pass every codebook rule", { clean_df <- readr::read_csv( here::here("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv"), col_types = voles_col_types() ) agent <- validate_voles(clean_df, "Clean data") expect_true(pointblank::all_passed(agent)) }) ``` ::: Run with `testthat::test_file(here::here("tests", "test_cleaning.R"))`. **3. Audit the logs against the data.** The cleaning log was written by the agent, so check it rather than trust it: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R ---- library(tidyverse) library(here) source(here("scripts", "functions", "validate_voles.R")) to_long <- function(data, value_name) { data |> pivot_longer( -raw_row, names_to = "column", values_to = value_name, values_transform = as.character ) } raw_long_df <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"), col_types = voles_col_types()) |> mutate(raw_row = as.character(row_number())) |> to_long("raw_value") clean_long_df <- read_csv(here("data", "derived", "voles_clean.csv"), col_types = voles_col_types()) |> to_long("clean_value") cleaning_log_df <- read_csv( here("data", "derived", "cleaning_log.csv"), col_types = cols(.default = col_character()) ) # 1. Truthful: every logged old value matches the raw file ---- untruthful_df <- cleaning_log_df |> left_join(raw_long_df, by = c("raw_row", "column")) |> filter(!map2_lgl(old_value, raw_value, identical)) # 2. Complete: every changed cell appears in the log ---- unlogged_df <- clean_long_df |> left_join(raw_long_df, by = c("raw_row", "column")) |> filter(!map2_lgl(clean_value, raw_value, identical)) |> anti_join(cleaning_log_df, by = c("raw_row", "column")) untruthful_df unlogged_df # 3. What kinds of change were made ---- cleaning_log_df |> count(column, rule, sort = TRUE) # 4. Ten logged changes to check by hand against the raw file ---- set.seed(2026) cleaning_log_df |> slice_sample(n = 10) ``` ::: `untruthful_df` and `unlogged_df` should both have zero rows. An unlogged change is the most dangerous outcome in this block: a value altered with no record. If a row appears, inspect it; a difference in number formatting is harmless, a changed value is not. For the ten sampled changes, open the raw file yourself and confirm each one. **4. Grade the pipeline against the planted errors.** Your instructor will now release the answer key. For each planted error, record: | Planted error | Failed validation on raw? | Handled as intended? | In the log? | |---|---|---|---| | | | | | The first column measures your *rules*; the second measures the *cleaning*; the third measures the *record*. A planted error that passed validation on raw data is a hole in your codebook, whatever the cleaning did. ## Debrief 1. Which planted errors did the AI's first draft of the codebook miss before you gave it the data provider's note? What does that say about who should own the codebook? 2. What did the agent do with the mass recorded in kilograms and the value ten times too large? If it "corrected" them, on whose authority? If the provider confirms a kilogram entry, the correction becomes a codebook rule you add, not something the script infers. 3. Which of your checks would have caught a script that set every mass to `NA`? 4. Once the clean output is right, freeze it as a reference, as in the [characterisation-test block](11i-characterisation-tests.qmd), so a later refactor of `01_clean.R` must reproduce it exactly. ## Check your understanding **Why must the codebook be written or confirmed by the analyst rather than inferred by the AI from the data?**
**Your validation rules all pass on the raw data before any cleaning. What is the most likely explanation in this exercise?**
**How does the checksum test differ from the permission deny rule?**
## References - Spreafico, M., Tassini, L., Sancricca, C. and Cappiello, C. (2025) 'Lost in the pipeline: how well do large language models handle data preparation?', arXiv preprint 2511.21708. - Claude Code documentation: *Extend Claude Code*, ; *Skills*, ; *Configure permissions*, . - Posit Assistant documentation: *Skills*, . :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Instructor only: generating the planted data Keep this script and `planted_errors.csv` **outside** the participant repository. An agent that can read the answer key will use it. Run it in an instructor copy of the repository that holds the clean `data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv`, and copy only the generated `data/raw/voles_raw.csv` into the participant repository. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # instructor/make_dirty_voles.R ---- library(tidyverse) library(here) # suppressWarnings: case_when() evaluates every branch, including numeric # conversion of text labels as_num <- function(x) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x)) clean_df <- read_csv( here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"), col_types = cols(.default = col_character()) ) plants_df <- tribble( ~row, ~column, ~error_class, 5, "mass_post_g", "sentinel 9999", 41, "mass_post_g", "sentinel 9999", 12, "metabolic_rate_post", "non-standard missing code -1", 20, "treatment_arm", "label in lower case", 33, "treatment_arm", "label in upper case", 58, "sex", "label spelled out", 27, "mass_pre_g", "recorded in kg", 64, "mass_pre_g", "decimal slip (x10)" ) |> mutate( subject_id = clean_df$subject_id[row], old_value = map2_chr(row, column, \(r, col) clean_df[[col]][[r]]), new_value = case_when( error_class == "sentinel 9999" ~ "9999", error_class == "non-standard missing code -1" ~ "-1", error_class == "label in lower case" ~ str_to_lower(old_value), error_class == "label in upper case" ~ str_to_upper(old_value), error_class == "label spelled out" ~ if_else(old_value == "M", "male", "female"), error_class == "recorded in kg" ~ as.character(as_num(old_value) / 1000), error_class == "decimal slip (x10)" ~ as.character(as_num(old_value) * 10) ) ) # apply each plant to its cell ---- planted_df <- reduce( seq_len(nrow(plants_df)), \(data, i) { data[[plants_df$column[[i]]]][[plants_df$row[[i]]]] <- plants_df$new_value[[i]] data }, .init = clean_df ) # insert an exact duplicate and a near duplicate with a malformed ID ---- near_duplicate_df <- planted_df |> slice(15) |> mutate(subject_id = str_replace(subject_id, "^V0", "V")) raw_df <- bind_rows( slice(planted_df, 1:30), slice(planted_df, 7), slice(planted_df, 31:50), near_duplicate_df, slice(planted_df, 51:n()) ) write_csv(raw_df, here("data", "raw", "voles_raw.csv"), na = "") # answer key, indexed by row in the raw file ---- key_df <- plants_df |> mutate( raw_row = row + (row > 30) + (row > 50), expected_handling = case_when( str_starts(error_class, "sentinel") | str_starts(error_class, "non-standard") ~ "recode to NA (codebook missing code); log", str_starts(error_class, "label") ~ "recode to canonical label; log", .default = "fails range rule; set to NA and query, do not infer a correction; log" ) ) |> select(raw_row, subject_id, column, old_value, new_value, error_class, expected_handling) |> bind_rows( tibble( raw_row = c(31, 52), subject_id = clean_df$subject_id[c(7, 15)], column = "(whole row)", error_class = c("exact duplicate row", "near duplicate: malformed ID"), expected_handling = c( "exclude one copy; log reason", "fails ID pattern; identify as duplicate of the original animal; exclude; log reason" ) ) ) write_csv(key_df, here("instructor", "planted_errors.csv")) ``` ::: The raw file has 74 rows: 72 animals, one exact duplicate (raw row 31) and one near duplicate (raw row 52). A correct pipeline excludes two rows and sets five values to `NA`: two sentinels, the `-1` code, and the two masses queried as out of range. These are in addition to the genuine missing value already in the source data. `docs/data_note.md` should state: IDs are V followed by three digits; sex is M or F; the three treatment arms; masses in grams, with adults in this colony between 15 and 60 g and 9999 entered when an animal could not be weighed; metabolic rate `-1` when the respirometry run failed, with valid readings between 5 and 30. :::
